sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.1 Measures of Location
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.locator: Section 1.3.5.1, Measures of Location, paragraphs on the mean, the median, and robustness to tail values

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that extreme tail values distort the mean while the rank-based median is not distorted by them, and that the median is the better location estimate for data with extreme tail values. No wording, example, dataset, or figure from the handbook is reproduced; the cohort, the clinic sample, and every worked calculation in this lesson are original.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.6 Measures of Scale
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.locator: Section 1.3.5.6, Measures of Scale, definitions of the range, the variance, the standard deviation, and the interquartile range

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the sample variance as the summed squared deviations from the mean divided by N minus 1, the standard deviation as its square root restoring the original data units while the variance squares them, the range as the largest minus the smallest value depending only on the two extremes, and the interquartile range as the seventy-fifth minus the twenty-fifth percentile describing variability near the centre. No wording, worked example, or dataset is reproduced; the participant, the two clinics, and every computed value are original.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.11 Measures of Skewness and Kurtosis
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.locator: Section 1.3.5.11, Measures of Skewness and Kurtosis, definition of skewness and of a symmetric data set

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that skewness measures the lack of symmetry, that a data set is symmetric when it looks the same to the left and to the right of its centre point, and that positive skewness means the right tail is long relative to the left. No wording, formula presentation, figure, or example data is reproduced.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.3.14.6 Histogram Interpretation: Skewed (Non-Normal) Right
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.locator: Section 1.3.3.14.6, the discussion of what counts as a typical value for symmetric and for skewed distributions and the recommendation on which summaries to report

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only as an introductory example of coincident centre summaries in a symmetric unimodal histogram, as an example of differing summaries in a displayed right-skewed histogram, and for the recommendation to report at least the mean and median for an inspected skewed distribution. The lesson does not treat the example as a general theorem: it states explicit existence, uniqueness, and unimodality conditions and supplies original counterexamples. No wording, histogram, dataset, or example is reproduced; the cohort, clinic sample, and every figure are original.

sources.title: Estimating the sample mean and standard deviation from the sample size, median, range and/or interquartile range
sources.locator: Background, on trials reporting the median with quartiles or with minimum and maximum; and the section deriving the interquartile range estimator, where the denominator converges to 2 times the inverse normal at 0.75, which is 1.34898

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that some medical trial reports give the median with the first and third quartiles or with the minimum and maximum instead of the mean and standard deviation, that the interquartile range is usually less sensitive to outliers than the range, and that for normal data the ratio of interquartile range to standard deviation converges to about 1.35. No formula derivation, table, simulation result, or wording is reproduced; the ratios computed in this lesson are calculated from its own invented data.

sources.title: Blood Glucose Test
sources.publisher: National Library of Medicine, National Institutes of Health
sources.locator: Section describing test preparation, on fasting before a fasting blood glucose test

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that a fasting blood glucose test requires the person to have gone without eating or drinking anything except water for at least eight hours before the sample. No wording, patient guidance, or reference range is reproduced, and this lesson asserts no diagnostic threshold.
